lehigh-2018-02.title: Fraction of the run
lehigh-2018-02.body:
The extra $\frac12$ mile is $\frac34-\frac23=\frac1{12}$ of the run, so the run is $12\cdot\frac12=6$ miles.

**Answer: 6**

lehigh-2018-04.title: Eliminate $y$
lehigh-2018-04.body:
From $\frac2x=\frac xy$: $y=\frac{x^2}{2}$. From $\frac y3=\frac xy$: $y^2=3x$. So $\frac{x^4}{4}=3x$, $x^3=12$, $x=\sqrt[3]{12}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt[3]{12}$**

lehigh-2018-04.title: Common ratio
lehigh-2018-04.body:
Call the common value $k$; then $x=\frac2k$, $y=3k$, $\frac xy=\frac2{3k^2}=k$, so $k^3=\frac23$ and $x=\frac2k=2\sqrt[3]{\frac32}=\sqrt[3]{12}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt[3]{12}$**

lehigh-2018-05.title: Multiply the factors
lehigh-2018-05.body:
The overall factor is $0.8^2\cdot1.2^2=(0.8\cdot1.2)^2=0.96^2=0.9216$, a change of $-7.84\%\approx-8\%$.

**Answer: $-8\%$ (an $8\%$ decrease)**

lehigh-2018-06.title: Two cases
lehigh-2018-06.body:
Either $x+3=3(x-2)$, giving $x=\frac92$, or $x+3=-3(x-2)$, giving $x=\frac34$. Both satisfy the equation. Sum: $\frac92+\frac34=\frac{21}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{21}{4}$**

lehigh-2018-07.title: Antifreeze balance
lehigh-2018-07.body:
Remove $x$ liters of the mixture and add $x$ liters of pure antifreeze: $0.4(6-x)+x=0.6\cdot6$, so $2.4+0.6x=3.6$, $x=2$.

**Answer: 2 liters**

lehigh-2018-08.title: Circumference vs radius
lehigh-2018-08.body:
Circumference is $2\pi r$, so adding $100$ feet to the circumference adds $\frac{100}{2\pi}\approx15.9$ feet to the radius, independent of the size of the earth. The poles are about $16$ feet high.

**Answer: 16 feet**

lehigh-2018-09.title: Area
lehigh-2018-09.body:
Two people eat area $\pi\cdot6^2=36\pi$, so four people eat $72\pi$, and each of three pizzas has area $24\pi=\pi(d/2)^2$. Then $d^2=96$, $d=4\sqrt6\approx9.8$ inches.

**Answer: $4\sqrt6$ inches**

lehigh-2018-10.title: Two right triangles
lehigh-2018-10.body:
Let the height be $h$. At first the distance is $h$ (45 degrees). After moving, the distance is $h+20$ and $\tan30^\circ=\frac h{h+20}=\frac1{\sqrt3}$. So $\sqrt3h=h+20$, $h=\frac{20}{\sqrt3-1}=10(\sqrt3+1)\approx27.3$.

**Answer: $10(\sqrt3+1)$ feet**

lehigh-2018-11.title: Replace $x$ by $-x$
lehigh-2018-11.body:
The second property with $x\to-x$: $f(1-x)=4+f(-x)$. Substitute into the first: $f(x)+4+f(-x)=10$, so $f(x)+f(-x)=6$ for all $x$. With $x=100$ the answer is $6$.

**Answer: 6**

lehigh-2018-12.title: Divisibility
lehigh-2018-12.body:
A number with $n$ digits all $2$ is divisible by $9$ iff $9\mid2n$, i.e. $9\mid n$; it is divisible by $11$ iff $n$ is even (alternating digit sum is $0$ for even $n$, $2$ for odd $n$). So $n=18$ and the digit sum is $36$.

**Answer: 36**

lehigh-2018-13.title: British flag theorem
lehigh-2018-13.body:
For any point in a rectangle the sums of squares of distances to opposite corners are equal. If the distances to the corners are $5$ and $14$ (opposite) and $10$ (a third corner), the fourth distance $d$ satisfies $5^2+14^2=10^2+d^2$, so $d^2=25+196-100=121$ and $d=11$.

**Answer: 11**

lehigh-2018-13.title: Perpendicular distances
lehigh-2018-13.body:
Let $A,B,C,D$ be the distances to the four sides in order around the rectangle. Then $A^2+B^2=5^2$, $B^2+C^2=10^2$, $C^2+D^2=14^2$, and the requested distance is $\sqrt{A^2+D^2}$. Adding the first and third and subtracting the second: $A^2+D^2=25+196-100=121$.

**Answer: 11**

lehigh-2018-14.title: Binomial expansion
lehigh-2018-14.body:
The expression is $(29+1)^4=30^4=2^4\cdot3^4\cdot5^4$, which has $(4+1)^3=125$ divisors.

**Answer: 125**

lehigh-2018-15.title: Rhombus minus sector
lehigh-2018-15.body:
Let the base be $BC$ with midpoint $O$ (the circle's center, radius $1$). The circle meets $AB$ and $AC$ again at $M$ and $N$; triangle $OBM$ is equilateral (since $OB=OM=1$, $\angle B=60^\circ$), so $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, and likewise $N$ is the midpoint of $AC$. Then $OMAN$ is a rhombus of side $1$ with angle $60^\circ$ at $O$, made of two unit equilateral triangles: area $\frac{\sqrt3}2$. The part of the triangle outside the circle is this rhombus minus the $60^\circ$ sector $OMN$ (area $\frac\pi6$).

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-\frac\pi6$**

lehigh-2018-17.title: A quartic with four equal values
lehigh-2018-17.body:
Let $f(x)=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx$. The equations say $f(1)=f(2)=f(3)=f(4)=K$. Then $f(x)-K$ is a monic quartic with roots $1,2,3,4$: $x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx-K=(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)(x-4)$. The $x^2$ coefficient is the second elementary symmetric sum $1\cdot2+1\cdot3+1\cdot4+2\cdot3+2\cdot4+3\cdot4=35$. So $b=35$.

**Answer: 35**

lehigh-2018-17.title: Linear system
lehigh-2018-17.body:
Subtracting consecutive expressions gives $15+7a+3b+c=0$, $65+19a+5b+c=0$, $175+37a+7b+c=0$; subtracting again: $50+12a+2b=0$, $110+18a+2b=0$, so $60+6a=0$, $a=-10$, then $b=35$ (and $c=-50$).

**Answer: 35**

lehigh-2018-19.title: Split by the role of the leading 1
lehigh-2018-19.body:
The other five digits contain either (i) no other $1$, or (ii) exactly one more $1$.

(i) The $1$ is a single digit; the five other positions hold two pairs $x,x,y,y$ and a single $z$, all different from $1$ and each other: choose $\{x,y\}$ from $9$ digits ($\binom92=36$), $z$ from $7$ ($7$), arrange $\frac{5!}{2!2!}=30$: $36\cdot7\cdot30=7560$.

(ii) The $1$'s form a pair: choose the position of the second $1$ ($5$ ways), the other pair's digit $y\ne1$ ($9$), its positions among the remaining four ($\binom42=6$), and the two remaining single digits, different from each other and from $1,y$ ($8\cdot7=56$): $5\cdot9\cdot6\cdot56=15120$.

Total $7560+15120=22680$.

**Answer: 22680**

lehigh-2018-20.title: Coordinates
lehigh-2018-20.body:
Center at the origin, the point at $(a,b)$. The circle points are $(a,b+2)$ and $(a-6,b)$: $a^2+(b+2)^2=50$ and $(a-6)^2+b^2=50$. Subtract the expanded forms: $a^2+b^2+4b=46$ and $a^2+b^2-12a=14$, so $4b+12a=32$, $b=8-3a$. Then $10a^2-60a+50=0$, $a=1$ or $5$: $(1,5)$ or $(5,-7)$. The second has $25+49=74>50$, outside. So the point is $(1,5)$, at distance $\sqrt{26}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{26}$**

lehigh-2018-22.title: Set up
lehigh-2018-22.body:
Let the number be $d\cdot10^k+m$ with $d$ the leading digit and $m<10^k$ the rest. The condition $m=\frac15(d\cdot10^k+m)$ gives $4m=d\cdot10^k$, i.e. $m=d\cdot10^k/4$. For $k=1$: $4m=10d$, $m=2.5d$, so $d=2$, $m=5$: $25$. For $k\ge2$: $m=25d\cdot10^{k-2}<10^k$ requires $d\le3$, giving $125,250,375$ for $k=2$ and $1250,2500,3750$ for $k=3$. The smallest five are $25,125,250,375,1250$.

**Answer: 1250**

lehigh-2018-24.title: Equal perimeter and area
lehigh-2018-24.body:
Let the triangles have sides $a,a,16c$ and $b,b,18c$ (bases in ratio $8:9$; the labelling does not matter). Equal perimeters: $a+8c=b+9c=:s$, so $c=a-b$. Areas: $8c\sqrt{a^2-64c^2}=9c\sqrt{b^2-81c^2}$. Since $a^2-64c^2=(a-8c)s$ and $b^2-81c^2=(b-9c)s$, this gives $8\sqrt{a-8c}=9\sqrt{b-9c}$, i.e. $64(a-8c)=81(b-9c)$. Substituting $c=a-b$: $281a=298b$. The smallest integer solution is $a=298$, $b=281$, $c=17$: triangles $(298,298,272)$ and $(281,281,306)$, each with perimeter $868$.

**Answer: 868**

lehigh-2018-25.title: Order of 3 mod 1000
lehigh-2018-25.body:
$3^n\equiv3\pmod{1000}$ iff $3^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod{1000}$. The multiplicative order of $3$ modulo $1000$ is $100$ (mod $8$ the order is $2$; mod $125$ it is $100$), so $n-1$ must be a multiple of $100$ and the smallest $n>1$ is $101$ (confirmed by direct computation).

**Answer: 101**

lehigh-2018-27.title: Mass points
lehigh-2018-27.body:
By the angle bisector theorem $BD:DC=AB:AC=3:1$. Give $B$ mass $1$; then $C$ has mass $3$ and $D$ has mass $4$. For the midpoint of $AD$ to balance, $A$ has mass $4$. Then $P$ on $AC$ satisfies $AP:PC=m(C):m(A)=3:4$, so $AP=\frac37\cdot AC=\frac37$.

**Answer: $\frac37$**

lehigh-2018-27.title: Menelaus
lehigh-2018-27.body:
Apply Menelaus to triangle $ADC$ with the line through $B$, $M$ (midpoint of $AD$), $P$: $\frac{AM}{MD}\cdot\frac{DB}{BC}\cdot\frac{CP}{PA}=1$. Here $\frac{AM}{MD}=1$, $\frac{DB}{BC}=\frac34$, so $\frac{CP}{PA}=\frac43$, hence $AP=\frac37$.

**Answer: $\frac37$**

lehigh-2018-28.title: Quadratic sequence
lehigh-2018-28.body:
The product of two arithmetic sequences is quadratic in $n$: $x_n=\alpha+\beta n+\gamma n^2$. From $x_1=10$, $x_2=37$, $x_3=86$: $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=10$, $\alpha+2\beta+4\gamma=37$, $\alpha+3\beta+9\gamma=86$. Second differences are $22=2\gamma$, so $\gamma=11$, then $\beta=-6$, $\alpha=5$. $x_{11}=5-6\cdot11+11\cdot121=5-66+1331=1270$.

**Answer: 1270**

lehigh-2018-29.title: Track the domains
lehigh-2018-29.body:
$f$ is increasing on $(-1,1)$ with values in $(\frac16,\infty)$, and $f(x)<c$ iff $x<1-\frac1{3c}$. So $\mathrm{dom}(f^n)=\{x\in(-1,1):f(x)\in\mathrm{dom}(f^{n-1})\}$, and each domain is an interval $(-1,t_n)$ with $t_1=1$, $t_{n}=1-\frac1{3t_{n-1}}$ (as long as $t_{n-1}>\frac16$):

$t_2=\frac23$, $t_3=\frac12$, $t_4=\frac13$, $t_5=0$, and then $t_6=1-\frac1{3\cdot0}$ requires $f(x)<0$, impossible since $f>\frac16$. So $\mathrm{dom}(f^5)=(-1,0)$ and $\mathrm{dom}(f^6)=\varnothing$.

**Answer: 5**

lehigh-2018-30.title: Products of consecutive terms
lehigh-2018-30.body:
Multiplying by $a_{k-1}$: $a_ka_{k-1}=a_{k-1}a_{k-2}+4$. So $p_k=a_ka_{k-1}$ satisfies $p_k=p_{k-1}+4$ with $p_2=-196$, i.e. $p_k=-196+4(k-2)$. This is $0$ first at $k=51$. For $k\le50$, $p_k
e0$ so no earlier term is $0$, while $p_{51}=0$ with $p_{50}=-4
e0$ gives $a_{50}
e0$, hence $a_{51}=0$.

**Answer: 51**

lehigh-2018-31.title: Count seatings of family labels
lehigh-2018-31.body:
Number the 8 seats and treat members of a family as indistinguishable: $\frac{8!}{3!3!2!}=560$ arrangements. A person fails if both neighbours are from the same family. With families $A,B$ of size $3$, $C$ of size $2$:

- $A$ all in a block of three: $8\cdot\frac{5!}{3!2!}=80$ arrangements (middle member has two relatives as neighbours); same for $B$: $80$. $A$ and $B$ both blocks: $8\cdot3=24$.
- A person of the two-member family $C$ always has at most one relative as a neighbour, so only $A$ and $B$ can contain a bad person.

Bad arrangements: $80+80-24=136$. Probability $\frac{560-136}{560}=\frac{424}{560}=\frac{53}{70}$.

**Answer: $\frac{53}{70}$**

lehigh-2018-32.title: External angle bisector theorem
lehigh-2018-32.body:
The external bisector at $B$ divides side $AC$ externally in the ratio $BA:BC=5:7$: $\frac{FA}{FC}=\frac57$. Since $FA<FC$, $F$ lies beyond $A$ and $FC=FA+3$. So $7FA=5FA+15$, $FA=\frac{15}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac{15}{2}$**

lehigh-2018-32.title: Law of sines
lehigh-2018-32.body:
Let $\theta=\angle FBA$. In triangle $ABF$: $\frac{\sin F}5=\frac{\sin\theta}{x}$ with $x=AF$. In triangle $CBF$, $\angle FBC=180^\circ-\theta$ and $\frac{\sin F}7=\frac{\sin\theta}{x+3}$. Dividing: $\frac x5=\frac{x+3}7$, so $x=\frac{15}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{15}{2}$**

lehigh-2018-33.title: Count to 2047 then subtract
lehigh-2018-33.body:
Count such numbers up to $2047=2^{11}-1$. For numbers with an odd number $2k+1$ of bits, the $2k$ bits after the leading $1$ must contain at least $k$ ones: $\frac12\left(2^{2k}+\binom{2k}k\right)$ numbers. For an even number of bits, exactly half of the numbers qualify. Summing over all lengths $\le11$ gives $\frac12\left(2047+\binom00+\binom21+\binom42+\binom63+\binom84+\binom{10}5\right)=\frac12(2047+351)=1199$.

The $29$ numbers $2019,\dots,2047$ all begin with $111111$ (they are at least $2016$), so they all qualify. Hence $1199-29=1170$.

**Answer: 1170**

lehigh-2018-34.title: Isosceles triangles
lehigh-2018-34.body:
$BO$ bisects $\angle B$ and $DE\parallel BC$, so $\angle DOB=\angle OBC=\angle OBD$ and $DB=DO$. Similarly $EC=EO$. So the perimeter of $ADE$ is $AD+DO+OE+EA=AD+DB+EC+EA=AB+AC=17$. Triangle $ADE\sim ABC$ with perimeter ratio $\frac{17}{24}$, hence $DE=\frac{17}{24}\cdot7=\frac{119}{24}$.

**Answer: $\frac{119}{24}$**

lehigh-2018-35.title: Geometric series of circles
lehigh-2018-35.body:
$P=(\sqrt2,0)$ and the tangent lines are $x\pm y=\sqrt2$. A circle centered at $(c,0)$ tangent to them has radius $\frac{\sqrt2-c}{\sqrt2}$. The first circle has center $(1+r,0)$ and is tangent to the unit circle: $r=\frac{\sqrt2-1-r}{\sqrt2}$, so $r=\frac{\sqrt2-1}{\sqrt2+1}=3-2\sqrt2$. In a wedge of half-angle $45^\circ$ successive tangent circles have constant radius ratio $\frac{1-\sin45^\circ}{1+\sin45^\circ}=3-2\sqrt2=r$. The areas form a geometric series: $\frac{\pi r^2}{1-r^2}$. With $r^2=17-12\sqrt2$ and $1-r^2=4(3\sqrt2-4)$ this equals $\frac{\pi(3\sqrt2-4)}8$.

**Answer: $\frac\pi8(3\sqrt2-4)$**

lehigh-2018-36.title: Recursion on the first play
lehigh-2018-36.body:
Let $p$ be the desired probability. On the first play both succeed with probability $\frac1{100}$ (then the counts are equal). Exactly one succeeds with probability $2\cdot\frac1{10}\cdot\frac9{10}=\frac{18}{100}$; the other must then succeed on the second play: probability $\frac1{10}$. Neither succeeds with probability $\frac{81}{100}$, after which the situation restarts. So $p=\frac1{100}+\frac{18}{1000}+\frac{81}{100}p$, $\frac{19}{100}p=\frac{28}{1000}$, $p=\frac{28}{190}=\frac{14}{95}$.

**Answer: $\frac{14}{95}$**

lehigh-2018-37.title: Chord lengths
lehigh-2018-37.body:
With $\theta=\pi/n$ and circumradius $R$: $A_1A_2=2R\sin\theta$, $A_1A_3=2R\sin2\theta$, $A_1A_4=2R\sin3\theta$. The condition becomes $\frac1{\sin\theta}=\frac1{\sin2\theta}+\frac1{\sin3\theta}$, i.e. $\sin2\theta\sin3\theta=\sin\theta(\sin2\theta+\sin3\theta)$. Dividing by $\sin\theta$: $2\cos\theta\sin3\theta=\sin2\theta+\sin3\theta$. Since $2\cos\theta\sin3\theta=\sin4\theta+\sin2\theta$, this reduces to $\sin4\theta=\sin3\theta$, so $4\theta=\pi-3\theta$ (the other branch $4\theta=3\theta+2k\pi$ is impossible), $\theta=\frac\pi7$, $n=7$.

**Answer: 7**

lehigh-2018-38.title: Parity and factoring
lehigh-2018-38.body:
If $p+q=r$ with $r>2$ then $r$ is odd, so exactly one of $p,q$ is $2$. If $q=2$ then $(r-p)(q-p)-279p=2(2-p)-279p<0$ is not a square, so $p=2$ and $r=q+2$. The expression is $q(q-2)-558=x^2$, i.e. $(q-1)^2-x^2=559=13\cdot43$. Hence $(q-1-x,\,q-1+x)=(13,43)$ or $(1,559)$, giving $q-1=28$ or $280$, $q=29$ or $281$. Then $r=31$ or $283$, both prime.

**Answer: $\{2,29,31\}$ and $\{2,281,283\}$**

lehigh-2018-39.title: Weighted AM-GM
lehigh-2018-39.body:
For $t>0$: $ab\le\frac t2a^2+\frac1{2t}b^2$, $bc\le\frac12b^2+\frac12c^2$, $cd\le\frac1{2t}c^2+\frac t2d^2$. Choose $t=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$, so $t^2=t+1$, i.e. $\frac1{2t}+\frac12=\frac t2$. Adding: $ab+bc+cd\le\frac t2(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)$. Equality holds for $b=ta$, $b=c$, $c=td$, so the maximum is $\frac t2=\frac{\sqrt5+1}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt5+1}{4}$**

lehigh-2018-40.title: Square
lehigh-2018-40.body:
The equation says $\sin2x=-(\sin x+\cos x)$. Squaring: $\sin^22x=1+\sin2x$, so $\sin2x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}2$; only $\frac{1-\sqrt5}2$ has absolute value at most $1$. Then $\sin x\cos x=\frac{1-\sqrt5}4$ and $u=\sin^2x$ satisfies $u(1-u)=\frac{6-2\sqrt5}{16}$, so $u=\frac12\pm\frac14\sqrt{2(\sqrt5-1)}$. The larger root gives $\sin x=\sqrt{\frac12+\frac14\sqrt{2(\sqrt5-1)}}=\frac12\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2(\sqrt5-1)}}\approx0.945$ (with $\cos x\approx-0.327$, which satisfies the original equation).

**Answer: $\frac12\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2(\sqrt5-1)}}$**
